To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) oxidative DNA damage is a common consequence of exposure to teratogenic agents; (ii) the embryo is susceptible to oxidative DNA damage, and this susceptibility is influenced by the stage of development; (iii) the embryo has the capacity to repair oxidative DNA damage, but this capacity is not always adequate to prevent developmental deficits; (iv) some proteins that are important for the detection of and signaling in response to oxidative DNA damage can protect the embryo from developmental deficits, while other such proteins

the most abundant oxidative DNA lesion 8-oxo-7,8-dihydroguanine is formed in embryos by ROS generated by xenobiotic exposure or endogenously, that this lesion is mutagenic and can alter transcription in vitro, and that 8-oxodG is repaired by base excision repair in embryos.
oxidative DNA damage and repair play important roles in teratogenesis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the mechanisms of teratogenesis and the neurodevelopmental deficits that result from oxidative damage to DNA.
the roles of oxidative DNA damage and repair, and related factors, in teratogenesis.

understanding the roles that oxidative DNA damage plays in embryotoxicity and neurodevelopmental disorders, including fetal alcohol spectrum disorders, autism, schizophrenia, attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, and others.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
oxidative DNA damage can be a significant contributor to the embryopathic effects of teratogens and can contribute to neurodevelopmental deficits in the absence of exogenous exposure.
oxidative DNA damage and repair are involved in teratogenesis, but the precise nature of this involvement and its relationship to other mechanisms of teratogenesis is still being defined.
oxidative DNA damage is a significant contributor to the etiology of some developmental disorders.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the embryo can be protected from the teratogenicity of ROS by the presence of key pathways for ROS detoxification and DNA damage detection/ signaling and repair, but that the embryo is not always protected by these factors, even in the presence of a teratogenic agent that can initiate the formation ROS.
DNA damage and repair are important for normal development.

oxidative DNA damage is a common mechanism of action for a wide range of teratogenic agents and that DNA repair can protect against the embryopathic consequences of such agents, but that there are important exceptions to this generalization that need to be understood.
The main takeaway from our work is that
oxidative damage to DNA is a major contributor to teratogenesis and that the embryo is highly vulnerable to oxidative stress.

the embryo can be adversely affected by oxidative DNA damage, that the embryo can protect itself from this damage, and that the mechanisms for protection may be similar or distinct from mechanisms of protection from other forms of DNA damage.

oxidative DNA damage can contribute to teratogenesis and developmental neurodeficits, but that this contribution may be variable depending upon the nature of the agent, the stage of embryonic development, and the genetic background of the embryo.
